question: The Texas Real Estate Commission itself is composed of how many appointed members, and in what mix?
choice_a: Nine members total: six licensed brokers and three public members
choice_b: Seven members total: five licensed brokers and two public members
choice_c: Nine members total: all nine must be licensed brokers
choice_d: Five members total: three licensed brokers and two public members
explanation: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.051 establishes a nine-member Commission consisting of six members who have been engaged in the brokerage business as licensed brokers as their major occupation, and three members who represent the public.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.051 (Commission Membership)

question: To qualify as one of the six broker-member seats on the Texas Real Estate Commission, an appointee must have:
choice_a: Been engaged in the brokerage business as a licensed broker as their major occupation for the five years preceding appointment
choice_b: Held a broker license for at least one year, with no occupational requirement
choice_c: Never previously served on any TREC advisory committee
choice_d: Been nominated exclusively by the Texas Association of Realtors
explanation: Section 1101.051 requires the six broker members of the Commission to have been engaged in the brokerage business as licensed brokers as their major occupation for the five years preceding their appointment by the governor.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.051 (Commission Membership)

question: A person is generally disqualified from serving as one of TREC's three public members if that person (or their spouse) is:
choice_a: Registered, certified, or licensed by an occupational regulatory agency in the real estate industry
choice_b: A registered voter residing in Texas
choice_c: Employed in any occupation unrelated to real estate
choice_d: A homeowner who has purchased residential property through a licensed broker
explanation: Section 1101.052 disqualifies a person from public-member appointment if the person or the person's spouse is registered, certified, or licensed by an occupational regulatory agency in the real estate industry, is employed by or participates in management of a commission-regulated entity, or owns more than a 10 percent interest in such an entity -- ensuring public members remain independent of the regulated industry.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.052 (Public Member Eligibility)

question: Under TREC's public-member eligibility restrictions, a person is also disqualified from appointment if that person or their spouse:
choice_a: Owns or controls, directly or indirectly, more than a 10 percent interest in a business entity regulated by or receiving funds from the Commission
choice_b: Has ever taken a TREC-approved continuing education course
choice_c: Resides in the same county as a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Has a child who attended a real estate pre-licensing course
explanation: Section 1101.052 bars appointment of a public member whose ownership interest -- individually or through a spouse -- exceeds 10 percent in a business entity or organization regulated by, or receiving funds from, the Commission, reinforcing the independence of the Commission's non-industry seats.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.052 (Public Member Eligibility)

question: Texas Real Estate Commission members serve terms structured as:
choice_a: Staggered six-year terms, with the terms of three members expiring on January 31 of each odd-numbered year
choice_b: A single, non-renewable two-year term for every member
choice_c: Lifetime appointments subject only to voluntary resignation
choice_d: Concurrent four-year terms that all expire simultaneously
explanation: Section 1101.055 staggers Commission membership by having the terms of three of the nine members expire on January 31 of each odd-numbered year, with each term lasting six years, which preserves institutional continuity as membership turns over gradually.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.055 (Terms; Vacancy)

question: A person who serves as an officer, employee, or paid consultant of a Texas trade association in the real estate industry is:
choice_a: Barred from serving as a Commission member or as a Commission employee in a bona fide executive, administrative, or professional capacity
choice_b: Given priority consideration for appointment to one of the six broker seats
choice_c: Automatically eligible to serve as one of the three public members
choice_d: Only restricted if the association is headquartered outside Texas
explanation: Section 1101.053 prohibits a person from serving as a Commission member (or in specified Commission staff roles) if that person -- or that person's spouse -- is an officer, employee, or paid consultant of a Texas trade association in the real estate industry, avoiding conflicts between industry-group interests and Commission governance.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.053 (Membership and Employment Restrictions)

question: A person required to register as a lobbyist under Chapter 305 of the Government Code because of compensated activities on behalf of a real-estate-related profession is:
choice_a: Barred from serving as a Commission member or as the Commission's general counsel
choice_b: Required to register as a lobbyist a second time before joining any TREC advisory committee
choice_c: Permitted to serve as a Commission member only if they resign their lobbying registration after appointment
choice_d: Subject to no restriction, since lobbying and Commission service are unrelated
explanation: Section 1101.053 bars a registered lobbyist for a profession related to the Commission's operation from serving as a Commission member or acting as the Commission's general counsel, separating advocacy roles from Commission governance and legal representation.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.053 (Membership and Employment Restrictions)

question: Among the baseline eligibility requirements Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.354 imposes on every license applicant (sales agent or broker) is that the applicant must:
choice_a: Be at least 18 years of age and be a United States citizen or a lawfully admitted alien
choice_b: Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited university
choice_c: Have resided in Texas for at least ten consecutive years
choice_d: Already hold a real estate license issued by another state
explanation: Section 1101.354 sets baseline eligibility for any license applicant, requiring the person to be at least 18 years old and either a U.S. citizen or a lawfully admitted alien, in addition to satisfying the Commission as to honesty, trustworthiness, and integrity, passing the required examination, and completing required coursework.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.354 (General Eligibility Requirements)

question: Before formally applying for a Texas real estate license, a prospective applicant may ask TREC to make an early determination of their eligibility by:
choice_a: Requesting a determination of fitness to engage in the profession and paying the required fee, with TREC required to notify the person of its determination within 30 days
choice_b: Filing a lawsuit in district court seeking declaratory relief
choice_c: Submitting an anonymous inquiry that TREC is required to answer within 24 hours
choice_d: There is no such pre-application option under Texas law
explanation: Section 1101.353 allows a person to request, before applying and upon payment of the required fee, that TREC determine whether the person possesses the fitness to engage in the profession, with TREC required to notify the person of its determination no later than the 30th day after making it -- a useful option for someone with a criminal history or other concern who wants clarity before investing in coursework.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.353 (Eligibility Determination)

question: If a person previously received a fitness determination from TREC and later actually applies for a license, TREC's review of that later application may include:
choice_a: A supplemental fitness determination, but one limited to covering only the period after the date of the original fitness-determination request
choice_b: A complete re-investigation reaching back to the applicant's birth with no time limitation
choice_c: Automatic license issuance with no further review of any kind
choice_d: Referral to a different state's licensing agency for a final decision
explanation: Section 1101.353 permits TREC to conduct a supplemental fitness determination when a person applies after receiving an earlier fitness determination, but that supplemental review may cover only the period following the date the person originally requested the fitness determination, avoiding re-litigating matters already resolved.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.353 (Eligibility Determination)

question: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.356 measures the experience requirement for a broker license applicant as:
choice_a: At least four years of active experience as a license holder during the 60 months preceding the date the application is filed
choice_b: Exactly four consecutive calendar years immediately before applying, with no other time frame permitted
choice_c: Two years of active experience, doubled only for applicants under age 25
choice_d: Ten years of active experience regardless of when it occurred
explanation: Section 1101.356 requires at least four years of active experience as a license holder within the 60 months (five years) preceding the filing of the broker application -- meaning the qualifying experience need not be the most recent four years or be perfectly consecutive, so long as it falls within that five-year window.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.356 (Broker License Requirements)

question: The broker qualifying and related education a Texas broker applicant must complete under Section 1101.356 is capped, by statute, at no more than:
choice_a: 60 semester hours, or the equivalent classroom hours, of qualifying real estate and related courses
choice_b: 12 semester hours, identical to the sales agent requirement
choice_c: 6 semester hours of any college-level coursework
choice_d: There is no statutory ceiling on required hours; TREC may require any number
explanation: Section 1101.356 directs TREC to require, by rule, the number of hours of qualifying real estate and related courses a broker applicant must complete, but caps that requirement at not more than 60 semester hours or the equivalent classroom hours -- the basis for TREC's current 900-classroom-hour broker education requirement.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.356 (Broker License Requirements)

question: A broker applicant's completion of the broker responsibility course approved under Section 1101.458 may be used to:
choice_a: Satisfy part of the related course hours required for the broker license itself
choice_b: Replace the entire 60-month active experience requirement
choice_c: Exempt the applicant from ever taking the broker licensing examination
choice_d: Substitute for the honesty, trustworthiness, and integrity determination
explanation: Section 1101.356 specifically allows the broker responsibility course approved under Section 1101.458 to be counted toward satisfying part of a broker applicant's required related course hours, rather than functioning as a wholly separate, additional requirement layered on top.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.356 (Broker License Requirements)

question: By contrast with the broker education requirement, a sales agent applicant under Section 1101.358 must complete qualifying real estate courses totaling at least:
choice_a: 12 semester hours, or the equivalent classroom hours, as required by commission rule
choice_b: 60 semester hours, the same total required of broker applicants
choice_c: 36 semester hours, exactly triple the sales agent minimum
choice_d: No fixed minimum; each course provider sets its own hour requirement
explanation: Section 1101.358 sets the sales agent education floor at 12 semester hours, or the equivalent classroom hours, of qualifying real estate courses -- substantially less than the broker applicant's 60-semester-hour ceiling, reflecting the sales agent's role operating under a sponsoring broker's supervision.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.358 (Sales Agent Education Requirements)

question: TREC may waive the sales agent qualifying education requirement under Section 1101.358 for an applicant who:
choice_a: Held a broker or sales agent license in Texas within the six months before filing the new application
choice_b: Has never been licensed in any state
choice_c: Is related by blood to a currently licensed Texas broker
choice_d: Passed a real estate course in high school more than six months earlier
explanation: Section 1101.358 permits TREC to waive the sales agent education requirement for an applicant who held a Texas broker or sales agent license within the six months preceding the new application, recognizing that such an applicant's coursework is unlikely to be stale.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.358 (Sales Agent Education Requirements)

question: Under Section 1101.451, TREC may issue or renew a Texas real estate license for a period of up to:
choice_a: 24 months
choice_b: 6 months
choice_c: 60 months
choice_d: 12 months, with no option for a longer term
explanation: Section 1101.451 authorizes TREC to issue or renew a license for a period of up to 24 months, establishing the standard two-year licensing and renewal cycle used throughout the chapter.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.451 (License Term)

question: A Texas licensee who lets their license lapse and applies to renew it within 90 days after expiration must generally pay a late renewal fee equal to:
choice_a: 1-1/2 times the normal required renewal fee
choice_b: Exactly the normal renewal fee, with no penalty for the first 90 days
choice_c: Five times the normal renewal fee
choice_d: A flat $10,000 reinstatement penalty
explanation: Section 1101.451 sets the late renewal fee at 1-1/2 times the normal renewal fee for a license renewed within 90 days after its expiration date, the first tier of the statute's graduated late-renewal penalty structure.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.451 (License Term; Late Renewal Penalties)

question: A Texas licensee whose license has been expired for more than 90 days but less than six months may renew it only by paying a late fee equal to:
choice_a: Two times the normal required renewal fee
choice_b: 1-1/2 times the normal required renewal fee, identical to the first 90 days
choice_c: Three times the normal required renewal fee
choice_d: No fee increase applies until the license has lapsed a full year
explanation: Section 1101.451 escalates the late renewal fee to two times the normal renewal fee once a license has been expired for more than 90 days but less than six months, before the license becomes entirely unrenewable at the six-month mark.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.451 (License Term; Late Renewal Penalties)

question: Once a Texas real estate license has been expired for six months or longer, the former licensee generally must:
choice_a: Apply for a new license and satisfy current requirements, since the lapsed license can no longer simply be renewed
choice_b: Pay triple the renewal fee and the license is automatically reinstated
choice_c: Wait exactly one additional year and then renew at the standard fee
choice_d: Nothing; renewal remains available indefinitely at the standard fee
explanation: Section 1101.451 cuts off the late-renewal option once a license has been expired six months or longer; at that point the former licensee must obtain a new license by meeting the requirements and procedures for an original application, rather than simply paying a higher fee to renew the old one.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.451 (License Term; Late Renewal Penalties)

question: Section 1101.455 sets the statutory floor for continuing education required of a Texas license holder during each license period at not less than:
choice_a: 15 classroom hours
choice_b: 40 classroom hours
choice_c: 3 classroom hours
choice_d: There is no statutory floor; TREC sets any number it chooses
explanation: Section 1101.455 requires TREC to prescribe, by rule, the classroom hours of continuing education a license holder must complete each license period, but sets a statutory floor of at least 15 classroom hours as the baseline the Commission's rule cannot go below.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.455 (Continuing Education)

question: Of a license holder's required continuing education hours under Section 1101.455, at least how many hours must cover mandatory legal topics such as commission rules, fair housing law, agency law, and antitrust law?
choice_a: 8 hours
choice_b: 1 hour
choice_c: All required hours must cover legal topics, with no elective hours permitted
choice_d: 20 hours
explanation: Section 1101.455 requires that at least eight of the continuing education hours a license holder must complete provide current information on specified legal topics -- including Commission rules, fair housing laws, Property Code issues, agency law, and antitrust laws -- with the remainder available for elective subject matter.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.455 (Continuing Education)

question: Once TREC has set continuing education hours at the statutory floor, Section 1101.455 limits how much the Commission may later increase that requirement, capping any increase over the term of a license at:
choice_a: No more than three additional hours
choice_b: No more than fifty additional hours
choice_c: There is no cap on how much the Commission may increase the requirement
choice_d: Exactly one additional hour per year of licensure
explanation: Section 1101.455 restricts TREC from increasing the number of required continuing education classroom hours by more than three hours over the term of a license, limiting how aggressively the Commission can ratchet up the CE burden -- consistent with the commonly cited 18-hour total (15-hour floor plus up to a 3-hour increase).
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.455 (Continuing Education)

question: Under Section 1101.455, a daily classroom course segment offered for continuing education credit must run:
choice_a: At least one hour and not more than ten hours
choice_b: Exactly eight hours, with no shorter or longer segments allowed
choice_c: At least one full week per segment
choice_d: No minimum or maximum length applies to any segment
explanation: Section 1101.455 requires that daily classroom course segments offered under the continuing education provisions run at least one hour and not more than ten hours, structuring how CE providers may schedule course days.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.455 (Continuing Education)

question: TREC's broker responsibility course, approved under Section 1101.458, may not exceed how many classroom hours, and which license holders must attend it?
choice_a: No more than six classroom hours, required of every licensed broker and of any sales agent who supervises another license holder
choice_b: No more than six classroom hours, required only of brokers who personally own their brokerage's office building
choice_c: No more than twenty classroom hours, required of every license holder regardless of role
choice_d: No more than six classroom hours, required only during a licensee's very first renewal cycle
explanation: Section 1101.458 caps the broker responsibility course at no more than six classroom hours and requires attendance not only by every licensed broker, but also by any sales agent who supervises another license holder -- such as a team leader -- reflecting the supervisory responsibilities both roles carry.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.458 (Broker Responsibility Course)

question: A sales agent who does not supervise any other license holder, and holds no broker license, is:
choice_a: Not subject to the broker responsibility course attendance requirement under Section 1101.458
choice_b: Still required to complete the broker responsibility course every renewal cycle regardless of supervisory role
choice_c: Required to complete twice the normal continuing education hours to compensate
choice_d: Barred from renewing their license until they complete the broker responsibility course
explanation: Section 1101.458 limits the mandatory broker responsibility course to licensed brokers and to sales agents who supervise another license holder; a non-supervising sales agent who is not a broker is outside that particular course requirement, though still subject to the general continuing education requirements of Section 1101.455.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.458 (Broker Responsibility Course)

question: Under Section 1101.651, a licensed sales agent's compensation for a real estate transaction must come from:
choice_a: The broker that is sponsoring the sales agent, or was sponsoring the sales agent when the compensation was earned
choice_b: Any party to the transaction directly, at the sales agent's discretion
choice_c: The buyer only, regardless of which party the sales agent represents
choice_d: A statewide compensation pool administered directly by TREC
explanation: Section 1101.651(b) prohibits a sales agent from accepting compensation for a real estate transaction from anyone other than the broker who is sponsoring the sales agent, or who was sponsoring the sales agent when the compensation was earned, preserving the broker's oversight of agent compensation.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651 (Compensation for Performance of Broker's Act)

question: A licensed sales agent who wants to pay a portion of a commission to another person must, under Section 1101.651, route that payment:
choice_a: Through the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent at that time
choice_b: Directly to the recipient, bypassing the sponsoring broker entirely
choice_c: Through the local MLS's escrow department
choice_d: Through TREC's central disbursement office
explanation: Section 1101.651(c) requires a sales agent to pay any commission only through the broker currently sponsoring that sales agent, reinforcing that a sales agent's brokerage-related payments and receipts flow through their sponsoring broker rather than directly between individuals.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651 (Compensation for Performance of Broker's Act)

question: A licensed Texas broker may lawfully pay compensation for performing an act of a broker to an unlicensed person only in the narrow circumstance where that person is:
choice_a: A real estate broker licensed in another state who does not conduct in Texas any of the negotiations for which the compensation is paid
choice_b: A close family member of the paying broker
choice_c: A former licensee whose license was revoked for cause within the past year
choice_d: Any unlicensed individual, provided the payment is disclosed in writing to all parties
explanation: Section 1101.651(a) generally bars a broker from compensating anyone for performing an act of a broker unless that person is a license holder, with a narrow exception for an out-of-state licensed broker who does not personally conduct any of the Texas-based negotiations for which the compensation is paid.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651 (Compensation for Performance of Broker's Act)
